topics.title: How do we assess democracy's outcomes?

concepts.label: Assessing Democracy's Outcomes
concepts.cardText: Democracy is seen as better than other forms of government because it promotes equality among citizens, enhances the dignity of the individual, improves the quality of decision-making, provides a method to resolve conflicts and allows room to correct mistakes. Most people support democracy, but not so many are satisfied with it in practice. The first step is to recognise that democracy is just a form of government: it can only create conditions for achieving something, and citizens have to take advantage of those conditions.
concepts.hint: Can a form of government achieve goals by itself, or does it create conditions?
concepts.probe: Why is democracy seen as good in principle but not so good in practice, and how should we assess its outcomes?
concepts.causeChain: High expectations that democracy will solve every problem -> unmet expectations -> people blame the idea of democracy; but democracy only creates conditions -> citizens must use those conditions to achieve goals

causeLinks.criterion: Connects democracy being just a form of government that creates conditions to why blaming democracy for every unmet expectation is a mistake.

keyPoints.text: We felt that democracy was better because it promotes equality among citizens, enhances the dignity of the individual, improves the quality of decision-making, provides a method to resolve conflicts and allows room to correct mistakes.
keyPoints.followUp: Why did we decide that democracy is better than other forms of government?

checks.criterion: Says democracy promotes equality among citizens.
Says democracy enhances the dignity of the individual.
Says democracy improves the quality of decision-making.
Says democracy provides a method to resolve conflicts.
Says democracy allows room to correct mistakes.

keyPoints.text: Most people support democracy against other alternatives, such as rule by a monarch or military or religious leaders. But not so many of them would be satisfied with the democracy in practice. So we face a dilemma: democracy is seen to be good in principle, but felt to be not so good in its practice.
keyPoints.followUp: What is the gap between how people view democracy as an idea and how they see it working?

requiredEvidence: not so good in its practice

checks.criterion: Explains the dilemma that democracy is seen as good in principle but not so good in practice.

keyPoints.text: Our fascination for democracy often pushes us into taking a position that democracy can address all socio-economic and political problems. The first step towards thinking carefully about the outcomes of democracy is to recognise that democracy is just a form of government. It can only create conditions for achieving something. The citizens have to take advantage of those conditions and achieve those goals.
keyPoints.followUp: Can democracy by itself solve all of a society's problems? What is its real role?

checks.criterion: States that democracy is just a form of government that can only create conditions for achieving goals, which citizens must take advantage of.

acceptedExamples: Over a hundred countries hold elections, have parties and guarantee rights, yet differ in social situations, economic achievements and cultures

misconceptions.wrong: Democracy should solve all of a country's socio-economic and political problems.
misconceptions.fix: Democracy is just a form of government. It can only create conditions for achieving something; citizens have to take advantage of those conditions.

verify.quote: Allows room to correct mistakes.
that democracy is just a form of government. It can only create conditions for achieving something.
The citizens have to take advantage of those conditions and achieve those goals.

concepts.label: Accountable Government and Transparency
concepts.cardText: The most basic outcome of democracy should be a government that is accountable to the citizens and responsive to their needs and expectations. Non-democratic rulers can decide quickly because they need not deliberate or worry about public opinion. Democracy is based on deliberation and negotiation, so some delay is bound to happen. But because it follows procedures, its decisions may be more acceptable to people and more effective, so the cost of time is perhaps worth it. Citizens also have the right and the means to examine how decisions are made; this is transparency.
concepts.hint: Is a fast decision always a good decision? What does following procedures give citizens?
concepts.probe: Does democracy produce a less efficient government? How does following procedures make it accountable?
concepts.causeChain: Democracy is based on deliberation and negotiation -> some delay -> but procedures are followed -> decisions more acceptable and effective, and citizens can examine the process (transparency) -> accountable government

causeLinks.criterion: Connects democracy taking more time to follow procedures to its decisions being more acceptable to the people and more effective.

keyPoints.text: In a democracy, people have the right to choose their rulers and control over the rulers, and citizens should be able to participate in decision making that affects them all. Therefore, the most basic outcome of democracy should be that it produces a government that is accountable to the citizens, and responsive to the needs and expectations of the citizens.
keyPoints.followUp: What is the most basic outcome we should expect from a democracy?

requiredEvidence: responsive to the needs and expectations

checks.criterion: States that the most basic outcome of democracy should be a government that is accountable to citizens and responsive to their needs and expectations.

keyPoints.text: Non-democratic rulers do not have to bother about deliberation in assemblies or worry about majorities and public opinion, so they can be very quick and efficient. Democracy is based on the idea of deliberation and negotiation, so some delay is bound to take place. But because the democratic government has followed procedures, its decisions may be both more acceptable to the people and more effective. So, the cost of time that democracy pays is perhaps worth it.
keyPoints.followUp: Why can non-democratic rulers act faster, and why are democratic decisions still often better?

requiredEvidence: more acceptable to the people and more effective

checks.criterion: Explains that democracy is based on deliberation and negotiation, so some delay is bound to happen, while non-democratic rulers can decide quickly.
States that because democratic decisions follow procedures, they may be more acceptable to the people and more effective, so the cost of time is worth it.

keyPoints.text: Democracy ensures that decision making will be based on norms and procedures. So, a citizen who wants to know if a decision was taken through the correct procedures can find this out. She has the right and the means to examine the process of decision making. This is known as transparency. This factor is often missing from a non-democratic government.
keyPoints.followUp: How can a citizen find out whether a decision was taken in the right way?

requiredEvidence: right and the means to examine

checks.criterion: Explains transparency: citizens have the right and the means to examine whether decisions were taken through the correct procedures.

acceptedExamples: Exercise: 'How does democracy produce an accountable, responsive and legitimate government?'

misconceptions.wrong: Democracy is worse than dictatorship because its decisions are slow.
misconceptions.fix: Some delay is bound to take place, but because democracy follows procedures, its decisions may be more acceptable to the people and more effective. The cost of time is perhaps worth it.

How does democracy produce an accountable, responsive and legitimate government?

concepts.label: The Record of Democratic Governments
concepts.cardText: To measure this outcome, look for regular, free and fair elections; open public debate on major policies; and citizens' right to information about the government. Democracies have done better at holding regular and free elections and allowing open debate, but fall short of giving everyone a fair chance and of debating every decision, and do not share much information with citizens. They often ignore the demands of a majority and are not free of corruption. Still, they are much better than non-democratic regimes, and nothing shows non-democracies are less corrupt.
concepts.hint: Where have democracies succeeded, and where do they fall short?
concepts.probe: What does the actual record of democracies show about accountability, responsiveness and corruption?
concepts.causeChain: Expected practices: free and fair elections, open debate, right to information -> democracies succeed on elections and debate, fall short on fair chances, information, responsiveness and corruption -> mixed record, but better than non-democratic regimes

keyPoints.text: To measure democracies on this outcome, you would look for regular, free and fair elections; open public debate on major policies and legislations; and citizens' right to information about the government and its functioning.
keyPoints.followUp: What would you look for to judge whether a democracy is accountable?

checks.criterion: Names regular, free and fair elections as a practice for measuring accountability.
Names open public debate on major policies and legislations.
Names citizens' right to information about the government and its functioning.

keyPoints.text: The actual performance of democracies shows a mixed record. Democracies have had greater success in setting up regular and free elections and conditions for open public debate. But most fall short of elections that provide a fair chance to everyone and of subjecting every decision to public debate, and do not have a very good record in sharing information with citizens. They are much better than any non-democratic regime in these respects.
keyPoints.followUp: How well have democracies actually done at meeting these standards? Where do they fall behind?

checks.criterion: Describes the mixed record: success in regular and free elections and open debate, but shortfalls in fair chances, public debate on every decision, or sharing information.

keyPoints.text: It may be reasonable to expect from democracy a government that is attentive to the needs and demands of the people and is largely free of corruption. The record of democracies is not impressive on these two counts. At the same time, there is nothing to show that non-democracies are less corrupt or more sensitive to the people.

checks.criterion: States that democracies' record on responsiveness and freedom from corruption is not impressive, but non-democracies are not less corrupt or more sensitive.

acceptedExamples: Exercise: Nannu filing an application under the Right to Information Act to get his duplicate ration card

misconceptions.wrong: Non-democratic governments are cleaner and more sensitive to people's needs.
misconceptions.fix: Democracies' record on corruption is not impressive, but there is nothing to show that non-democracies are less corrupt or more sensitive to the people.

concepts.label: Democracy as Legitimate Government
concepts.cardText: In one respect democratic government is certainly better than its alternatives: it is legitimate government. It may be slow, less efficient, not always very responsive or clean, but a democratic government is people's own government. That is why there is overwhelming support for the idea of democracy all over the world, including in South Asia, in countries with and without democratic regimes. People wish to be ruled by representatives elected by them. Democracy's ability to generate its own support is itself an outcome.
concepts.hint: Why do people support democracy even when it is slow or not very clean?
concepts.probe: In what respect is democratic government certainly better than its alternatives?
concepts.causeChain: Democratic government is people's own government -> legitimate -> overwhelming support for democracy, even where it is slow or not clean -> democracy generates its own support

causeLinks.criterion: Connects democratic government being people's own government to the overwhelming support for democracy around the world.

keyPoints.text: There is one respect in which democratic government is certainly better than its alternatives: democratic government is legitimate government. It may be slow, less efficient, not always very responsive or clean. But a democratic government is people's own government.
keyPoints.followUp: In what one respect is democratic government always better than its alternatives?

checks.criterion: States that democratic government is legitimate because it is people's own government, even if slow, less efficient or not always clean.

keyPoints.text: That is why there is an overwhelming support for the idea of democracy all over the world. Evidence from South Asia shows the support exists in countries with democratic regimes as well as countries without democratic regimes. People wish to be ruled by representatives elected by them, and believe democracy is suitable for their country. Democracy's ability to generate its own support is itself an outcome that cannot be ignored.
keyPoints.followUp: What does survey evidence show about how much people support democracy, even where they don't have it?

checks.criterion: Mentions the overwhelming support for democracy (for example in South Asia, in democratic and non-democratic countries), people wishing to be ruled by elected representatives.
States that democracy's ability to generate its own support is itself an outcome.

acceptedExamples: State of Democracy in South Asia survey: 95 per cent in India agree with the rule of leaders elected by the people

verify.quote: But a democratic government is people's own government.

concepts.label: Democracy and Economic Growth
concepts.cardText: In practice, many democracies did not produce development. Between 1950 and 2000, dictatorships had a slightly higher average rate of economic growth (4.42 against 3.95 per cent). But economic development depends on several factors: population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries and economic priorities. Among poor countries, the difference between dictatorships and democracies is negligible (4.34 against 4.28 per cent). We cannot say democracy guarantees development, but we can expect it not to lag behind dictatorships, and it has several other positive outcomes.
concepts.hint: Compare poor dictatorships with poor democracies. What else decides economic growth?
concepts.probe: Do dictatorships produce faster economic growth than democracies? Why is that no reason to reject democracy?
concepts.causeChain: Growth depends on population, global situation, cooperation and priorities, not only the form of government -> among poor countries the growth difference is negligible -> no reason to reject democracy, which has other positive outcomes

causeLinks.criterion: Connects economic development depending on many factors (population, global situation, cooperation, priorities) to the negligible difference between poor democracies and poor dictatorships.

keyPoints.text: If you consider all democracies and all dictatorships for the fifty years between 1950 and 2000, dictatorships have slightly higher rate of economic growth. Many democracies did not fulfil the expectation of development.

requiredEvidence: slightly higher rate of economic growth

checks.criterion: States that between 1950 and 2000, dictatorships on average had a slightly higher rate of economic growth than democracies.

keyPoints.text: Economic development depends on several factors: country's population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries, economic priorities adopted by the country, etc.
keyPoints.followUp: Which factors decide how fast a country's economy grows?

checks.criterion: Explains that economic development depends on several factors such as population size, the global situation, cooperation from other countries or economic priorities.

keyPoints.text: The difference in the rates of economic development between less developed countries with dictatorships and democracies is negligible (poor countries under dictatorship 4.34 per cent, under democracy 4.28 per cent). Overall, we cannot say that democracy is a guarantee of economic development. But we can expect democracy not to lag behind dictatorships, and it is better to prefer democracy as it has several other positive outcomes.
keyPoints.followUp: How do the growth rates of poor countries under dictatorships and under democracies compare?

checks.criterion: States that among poor countries the difference in growth between dictatorships and democracies is negligible.

concepts.label: Reduction of Inequality and Poverty
concepts.cardText: Democracies are based on political equality: every individual has equal weight in electing representatives. But economic inequalities are growing: a small number of ultra-rich enjoy a highly disproportionate and increasing share of wealth, while incomes of those at the bottom decline. In South Africa and Brazil, the top 20 per cent take over 60 per cent of national income. Democracies do not appear very successful in reducing economic inequalities; though the poor are a large share of voters, governments are not as keen to address poverty as expected. In Bangladesh, more than half the population lives in poverty.
concepts.hint: Every person has one vote. Does that mean wealth is shared equally?
concepts.probe: Why has political equality in democracies not led to a reduction in economic inequality and poverty?
concepts.causeChain: Political equality (equal weight in voting) -> but growing economic inequality: ultra-rich gain, bottom incomes decline -> poor are a large share of voters, yet governments not keen to address poverty -> democracies not very successful in reducing inequality

causeLinks.criterion: Contrasts political equality (equal votes) with growing economic inequality, explaining that one does not automatically produce the other.

keyPoints.text: Democracies are based on political equality. All individuals have equal weight in electing representatives. Parallel to this, we find growing economic inequalities. A small number of ultra-rich enjoy a highly disproportionate share of wealth and incomes, and their share has been increasing. Those at the bottom of the society have very little to depend upon; their incomes have been declining.
keyPoints.followUp: How does political equality in a democracy compare with the economic situation of its people?

checks.criterion: States that democracies are based on political equality, with all individuals having equal weight in electing representatives.
States that economic inequalities are growing: the ultra-rich have a disproportionate and increasing share, while incomes at the bottom decline.

keyPoints.text: In actual life, democracies do not appear to be very successful in reducing economic inequalities. The poor constitute a large proportion of our voters and no party will like to lose their votes. Yet democratically elected governments do not appear to be as keen to address the question of poverty as you would expect them to.
keyPoints.followUp: Why is it surprising that democracies have not done more about poverty?

requiredEvidence: not very successful in reducing economic inequalities

checks.criterion: States that democracies have not been very successful in reducing economic inequalities, and elected governments are not as keen on poverty as expected even though the poor are many voters.

keyPoints.text: In democratic countries like South Africa and Brazil, the top 20 per cent people take away more than 60 per cent of the national income, leaving less than 3 per cent for the bottom 20 per cent. Countries like Denmark and Hungary are much better. In Bangladesh, more than half of its population lives in poverty, and people in several poor countries depend on rich countries even for food supplies.

checks.criterion: Gives an example of inequality in democracies, such as the top 20 per cent taking over 60 per cent of national income in South Africa or Brazil.

acceptedExamples: Table 2: South Africa top 20 per cent 64.8, bottom 20 per cent 2.9; Denmark 34.5 and 9.6

concepts.label: Accommodation of Social Diversity
concepts.cardText: Democracies usually develop a procedure to conduct competition among groups, reducing the chance that tensions become explosive or violent. No society can fully resolve conflicts, but democracy is best suited to respecting differences and negotiating them, while non-democratic regimes often suppress them. Sri Lanka reminds us of two conditions: democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion, since the majority must work with the minority and majorities are not permanent; and rule by majority must not become rule by a majority community of religion, race or language. Every citizen must have a chance of being in the majority at some point.
concepts.hint: Is democracy just majority rule? What happens if someone can never be in the majority because of birth?
concepts.probe: Under what conditions do democracies accommodate social diversities?
concepts.causeChain: Democracy develops procedures for competition -> tensions less likely to turn violent -> differences negotiated; but only if majority works with minority and majority is not fixed by religion, race or language -> every citizen can be in the majority at some time

causeLinks.criterion: Connects democracy's procedures for negotiating differences to the condition that majority rule must not become rule by a fixed majority community.

keyPoints.text: Democracies usually develop a procedure to conduct their competition. This reduces the possibility of tensions becoming explosive or violent. No society can fully and permanently resolve conflicts among different groups, but we can learn to respect these differences and evolve mechanisms to negotiate them. Democracy is best suited to produce this outcome; non-democratic regimes often turn a blind eye to or suppress internal social differences.
keyPoints.followUp: How do democracies handle competition and conflict between social groups?

checks.criterion: Explains that democracies develop procedures to conduct competition among groups, reducing the chance of tensions becoming explosive or violent, and negotiate differences.
Mentions that non-democratic regimes often ignore or suppress internal social differences.

keyPoints.text: It is necessary to understand that democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion. The majority always needs to work with the minority so that governments function to represent the general view. Majority and minority opinions are not permanent.
keyPoints.followUp: Is democracy just the rule of the majority? How should the majority treat the minority?

requiredEvidence: not simply rule by majority opinion

checks.criterion: States the first condition: democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion; the majority must work with the minority, and majorities and minorities are not permanent.

keyPoints.text: It is also necessary that rule by majority does not become rule by majority community in terms of religion or race or linguistic group. In every decision or election, different persons and groups may form a majority. Democracy remains democracy only as long as every citizen has a chance of being in majority at some point of time. If someone is barred from being in majority on the basis of birth, then the democratic rule ceases to be accommodative for that person or group.
keyPoints.followUp: What must majority rule never turn into, for democracy to accommodate everyone?

requiredEvidence: religion or race or linguistic group

checks.criterion: States the second condition: rule by majority must not become rule by a majority community of religion, race or language; every citizen must have a chance of being in the majority.

acceptedExamples: Belgium successfully negotiating differences among ethnic populations
Sri Lanka as a reminder of the two conditions

misconceptions.fix: Democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion. The majority always needs to work with the minority, and majority and minority opinions are not permanent.

misconceptions.wrong: Democracy accommodates diversity by ending all conflicts between groups.

topics.title: Dignity and freedom of the citizens

concepts.label: Dignity and Freedom of the Citizens
concepts.cardText: Democracy is much superior to any other form of government in promoting the dignity and freedom of the individual; the passion for respect and freedom is the basis of democracy. Long struggles by women have made respect and equal treatment of women necessary ingredients of a democratic society. Women are not always treated with respect, but once the principle is recognised, it is easier to struggle against what is now unacceptable legally and morally. Democracy in India has also strengthened the claims of disadvantaged castes for equal status and opportunity.
concepts.hint: Does recognising equality in principle end discrimination at once? What does it make easier?
concepts.probe: How does democracy promote the dignity and freedom of women and of disadvantaged castes?
concepts.causeChain: Democracy recognises equality and dignity in principle -> discrimination becomes legally and morally unacceptable -> easier for women and disadvantaged castes to struggle for equal treatment

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the recognition of equality in principle to discrimination becoming legally and morally unacceptable, making it easier to struggle against it.

keyPoints.text: Democracy stands much superior to any other form of government in promoting dignity and freedom of the individual. Every individual wants to receive respect from fellow beings. The passion for respect and freedom are the basis of democracy.
keyPoints.followUp: How does democracy compare with other forms of government in respecting individuals?

requiredEvidence: dignity and freedom of the individual

checks.criterion: States that democracy is superior to other forms of government in promoting the dignity and freedom of the individual.

keyPoints.text: Long struggles by women have created some sensitivity today that respect to and equal treatment of women are necessary ingredients of a democratic society. That does not mean that women are actually always treated with respect. But once the principle is recognised, it becomes easier for women to wage a struggle against what is now unacceptable legally and morally. In a non-democratic set up, this unacceptability would not have legal basis.
keyPoints.followUp: How has democracy changed the way society thinks about treating women?

checks.criterion: Explains that women's struggles made equal treatment a recognised principle of democracy, even if women are not always treated with respect.
Explains that once the principle is recognised, discrimination becomes legally and morally unacceptable, so it is easier to struggle against it.

keyPoints.text: The same is true of caste inequalities. Democracy in India has strengthened the claims of the disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and equal opportunity. There are instances still of caste-based inequalities and atrocities, but these lack the moral and legal foundations.
keyPoints.followUp: How has democracy in India affected the claims of disadvantaged castes?

requiredEvidence: lack the moral and legal foundations

checks.criterion: States that democracy in India has strengthened the claims of disadvantaged castes for equal status and opportunity, and caste atrocities now lack moral and legal foundations.

acceptedExamples: Exercise: following a High Court directive, a temple in Orissa with separate doors for dalits and non-dalits allowed entry for all from the same door
Rosa Parks cartoon on the efficacy of the vote

misconceptions.fix: That does not mean they are always treated with respect. But once the principle is recognised, it becomes easier to struggle against what is now unacceptable legally and morally.

concepts.label: Democracy's Examination Never Gets Over
concepts.cardText: Expectations from democracy also work as criteria for judging any democratic country. Its examination never gets over: as democracy passes one test, it produces another, and as people get some benefits they ask for more. People's complaints are themselves a testimony to the success of democracy: they show awareness and the ability to look critically at power holders. Public dissatisfaction shows that democracy transforms people from the status of a subject into that of a citizen. Most people believe their vote makes a difference.
concepts.hint: If people keep complaining about democracy, is that a sign of failure or of success?
concepts.probe: Why does the textbook say that people's complaints about democracy are a sign of its success?

causeLinks.criterion: Connects people's complaints and expectations to the success of democracy in turning subjects into citizens.

keyPoints.text: What is most distinctive about democracy is that its examination never gets over. As democracy passes one test, it produces another test. As people get some benefits of democracy, they ask for more and want to make democracy even better.

checks.criterion: States that democracy's examination never gets over: as it passes one test, people expect more.

A public expression of dissatisfaction with democracy shows the success of the democratic project: it transforms people from the status of a subject into that of a citizen.
